en: Majjhima Nikāya 106,
Āneñjasappāyasutta:
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kurus at a Kuru town named Kammāsadhamma.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus!"
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, sensual pleasures are impermanent, empty, false, and subject to deception.”
“Bhikkhus, this is a fabrication of illusion, a mere prattle of fools:
the sensual pleasures pertaining to the present life and those pertaining to the future life,
as well as the perceptions of sensual pleasure pertaining to the present life and those pertaining to the future life.”
Both of these are Māra’s domain, this is Māra’s sphere, this is Māra’s bait, this is Māra’s range.
Herein, these evil unwholesome mental states—covetousness, ill will, and aggression—arise.
These very things become obstacles for a noble disciple who trains here in this Dhamma.
In this regard, monks, the noble disciple reflects thus:
‘There are sensual pleasures pertaining to the present life and sensual pleasures pertaining to future lives;
there is the perception of sensual pleasure pertaining to the present life and the perception of sensual pleasure pertaining to future lives.’
Both of these are Māra’s domain; this is Māra’s sphere, Māra’s bait, and Māra’s range.
It is here that these evil, unwholesome mental states—covetousness, ill will, and aggression—arise;
and these very things become obstacles for a noble disciple training here in this Dhamma.
"What if I were to dwell with a mind that is vast and exalted, having overcome the world and resolved upon it with my mind?

For as I dwell with a mind that is vast and exalted, having overcome the world and resolved upon it with my mind, those evil and unwholesome mental states—covetousness, ill will, and aggression—will not arise.
Through their abandonment, my mind will become non-limited, immeasurable, and well-developed."
As he practices in this way and dwells frequently therein, his mind becomes serene toward that sphere.

When there is such serenity, either he now enters into imperturbability or resolves with wisdom; and at the breaking up of the body, after death, it is possible that his consciousness will lead to rebirth in that state, reaching the imperturbable.
“Monks, this is declared to be the first practice conducive to imperturbability.
Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus:
‘There are sensual pleasures pertaining to the present life, and there are sensual pleasures pertaining to future lives;’”
“Whatever perception of sensual pleasure there is pertaining to the present life, and whatever perception of sensual pleasure there is pertaining to future lives;
whatever form there is—all form consists of the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements.
For one who practices in this way and dwells frequently therein, the mind becomes serene toward that sphere.

When there is confidence, one either enters into imperturbability now or resolves with wisdom; then, with the breakup of the body, after death, it is possible that his consciousness will lead to that and reach imperturbability.
This, monks, is declared to be the second practice conducive to imperturbability.
Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus:
‘There are sensual pleasures pertaining to the present life and sensual pleasures pertaining to future lives;
there is the perception of sensual pleasure pertaining to the present life and the perception of sensual pleasure pertaining to future lives.’
Whatever forms pertain to the present life and whatever forms pertain to future lives;
whatever perception of forms pertains to the present life and whatever perception of forms pertains to future lives—
all this is impermanent.
‘What is impermanent is not worth delighting in, not worth welcoming, not worth adhering to.
For one who practices in this way and dwells frequently therein, the mind becomes serene toward that sphere.
When there is such serenity, either one attains imperturbability in this very life, or else one is resolved through wisdom regarding the state after the breakup of the body, following death.
"It is possible that the consciousness leading thereto may become immovable.
This, monks, is declared to be the third way of practice conducive to the immovable.
Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus:"
‘Whatever sensual pleasures pertain to the present life and whatever sensual pleasures pertain to future lives;
whatever perceptions of sensual pleasure pertain to the present life and whatever perceptions of sensual pleasure pertain to future lives;
whatever forms pertain to the present life and whatever forms pertain to future lives;’
Whatever perception of form pertaining to the present life, whatever perception of form pertaining to future lives,
and whatever perception of the imperturbable—
all these are perceptions.
‘Where these [perceptions] cease without remainder, that is the peaceful,
that is the sublime— namely, the base of nothingness.
As he practices in this way and dwells frequently therein, his mind becomes serene toward that sphere.

When there is confidence, one either enters the base of nothingness now, or resolves with wisdom; then, with the breakup of the body, after death, it is possible that his consciousness will be such as to lead to rebirth in the base of nothingness.
This, monks, is declared to be the first practice conducive to the base of nothingness.
Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple, having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus:
"This is empty of a self or of anything belonging to a self.
As he practices in this way and dwells frequently therein, his mind becomes serene in that sphere.
When there is confidence, one either enters the base of nothingness now or resolves upon it with wisdom;
then, with the breakup of the body, after death, it is possible that his consciousness will be led toward rebirth in the base of nothingness.
This, monks, is declared to be the second practice conducive to the base of nothingness.
Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus:
"I am not anyone's anything anywhere, nor is there anything of mine belonging to anyone anywhere.
As he practices in this way and dwells frequently therein, his mind becomes serene in that sphere.
When there is serene confidence, one either enters the base of nothingness now, or resolves upon it with wisdom;
then, with the breakup of the body, after death, it is possible that the consciousness leading to that state will reach the base of nothingness.
This, monks, is declared to be the third practice conducive to the base of nothingness.
Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus:
‘There are sensual pleasures pertaining to the present life and sensual pleasures pertaining to future lives;
there is perception of sensual pleasure pertaining to the present life and perception of sensual pleasure pertaining to future lives.’
Whatever forms pertain to the present life and whatever forms pertain to future lives;
whatever perception of form pertains to the present life and whatever perception of form pertains to future lives;
and the perception of the imperturbable and the perception of the base of nothingness—
"All perceptions.
Where these cease without remainder— that is peaceful, that is sublime,
namely, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
As he practices in this way and dwells frequently therein, his mind becomes serene regarding that sphere.
When there is such serenity, either in this very life he enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, or he resolves upon it with wisdom;
or, with the breakup of the body, after death, it is possible that his consciousness will be reborn in accordance with that, reaching the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
“Monks, this is declared to be the practice conducive to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:
“In this case, Bhante, a bhikkhu practices in this way:”
‘Let there be nothing for me, and may nothing be mine; let there not be anything in the future, and may nothing belong to me in the future; whatever exists, whatever has come to be—that I abandon.
In this way, he attains equanimity.
“Would such a bhikkhu, venerable sir, attain final nibbāna, or would he not attain final nibbāna?”
“Ānanda, some bhikkhu here might attain final Nibbāna, while another bhikkhu here might not attain final Nibbāna.
“But what, Bhante, is the cause, what is the reason why some bhikkhu here might attain final Nibbāna, while another bhikkhu here might not attain final Nibbāna?
“Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu practices in this way:”
‘Let there be nothing for me, and may nothing be mine; let there not be anything in the future, and may nothing be mine in the future; whatever exists, whatever has come to be—that I abandon.
In this way, one attains equanimity.
One delights in that equanimity, welcomes it, and remains clinging to it.
“Ānanda, for one who delights in that equanimity, welcomes it, and remains clinging to it, consciousness becomes dependent upon it and takes it as its fuel.
A bhikkhu with such fuel, Ānanda, does not attain final Nibbāna.
“But where, Bhante, does that bhikkhu, while taking up, take up?”
“The base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, Ānanda.
“Venerable sir, that bhikkhu, it seems, while grasping, grasps at the best kind of clinging,” [he asked].
“For that bhikkhu, Ānanda, while grasping, grasps at the best kind of clinging,” [the Blessed One replied].
For this, Ānanda, is the supreme among acquisitions, namely,
the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu practices in this way:
‘Let there be nothing for me, and may nothing be mine; let there not be anything, and may nothing be mine in the future; whatever exists, whatever has come to be—that I abandon.
In this way, he attains equanimity.
He does not delight in that equanimity, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it.
“Since he does not delight in that equanimity, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it, his consciousness is not dependent upon it and does not grasp it.
Being without grasping, Ānanda, a bhikkhu attains final Nibbāna.
“It is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante!”
“Indeed, venerable sir, it is by relying on various supports that the Blessed One has taught the crossing over of the flood.
But what, venerable sir, is the noble liberation?
“In this case, Ānanda, a bhikkhu who is a noble disciple reflects thus:”
‘Those sensual pleasures pertaining to the present life and those pertaining to the future life;
that perception of sensual pleasure pertaining to the present life and that perception of sensual pleasure pertaining to the future life;
those forms pertaining to the present life and those pertaining to the future life;’
Whatever perception of form there is pertaining to the present life, and whatever perception of form there is pertaining to future lives;
whatever perception of the imperturbable, whatever perception of the base of nothingness, and whatever perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
this is identity (sakkāya), as far as identity extends.
This is the deathless: namely, the liberation of the mind through non-clinging.
Thus, Ānanda, I have taught the practice conducive to imperturbability; I have taught the practice conducive to the base of nothingness;
I have taught the practice conducive to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and I have taught, depending on each respective stage, how to cross over the flood.
“...the noble liberation has been taught as a means of crossing over.
Ānanda, whatever was to be done for disciples by a Teacher who seeks their welfare and is compassionate, out of compassion, that has been done by me for you.
Here, Ānanda, are the roots of trees; here are empty huts. Meditate, Ānanda, do not be negligent, lest you later fall into regret. This is our instruction to you.”
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The Venerable Ānanda, being uplifted, rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The sixth discourse, the Āneñjasappāyasutta, is concluded.
